claim: Mechanical ventilation is a critical intervention for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
source: Although mechanical ventilation is a critical intervention for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), it can trigger an IL-1β-associated complication known as ventilator-induced lung injury.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Mechanical ventilation can trigger an IL-1β-associated complication known as ventilator-induced lung injury.
source: Although mechanical ventilation is a critical intervention for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), it can trigger an IL-1β-associated complication known as ventilator-induced lung injury.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript and cited literature.

claim: In mice, lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and high-volume ventilation (LPS-HVV) lead to hypoxemia with neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) formation in the alveoli.
source: In mice, we found that lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and high-volume ventilation, LPS-HVV, lead to hypoxemia with neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) formation in the alveoli.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1, including PaO2 measurements and NETs markers.

claim: Il1r1-/- LPS-HVV mice did not develop hypoxemia.
source: Furthermore, Il1r1-/- LPS-HVV mice did not develop hypoxemia and had reduced NETs, indicating that IL-1R1 signaling is important for NETs formation and hypoxemia.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B comparing WT and Il1r1-/- mice.

claim: Il1r1-/- LPS-HVV mice had reduced NETs.
source: Furthermore, Il1r1-/- LPS-HVV mice did not develop hypoxemia and had reduced NETs, indicating that IL-1R1 signaling is important for NETs formation and hypoxemia.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4M measuring MPO-DNA complexes.

claim: IL-1R1 signaling is important for NETs formation and hypoxemia.
source: Furthermore, Il1r1-/- LPS-HVV mice did not develop hypoxemia and had reduced NETs, indicating that IL-1R1 signaling is important for NETs formation and hypoxemia.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that Il1r1-/- mice have reduced hypoxemia and NETs.

claim: Therapeutic hypothermia (TH) at 32°C body temperature prevented hypoxemia development in LPS-HVV mice.
source: In LPS-HVV mice, TH (32°C body temperature) prevented hypoxemia development, reducing albumin leakage, IL-1β, gasdermin D (GSDMD), and NETs formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C comparing normothermia and hypothermia groups.

claim: Therapeutic hypothermia at 32°C reduced albumin leakage in LPS-HVV mice.
source: In LPS-HVV mice, TH (32°C body temperature) prevented hypoxemia development, reducing albumin leakage, IL-1β, gasdermin D (GSDMD), and NETs formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F measuring albumin in BALF.

claim: Therapeutic hypothermia at 32°C reduced IL-1β in LPS-HVV mice.
source: In LPS-HVV mice, TH (32°C body temperature) prevented hypoxemia development, reducing albumin leakage, IL-1β, gasdermin D (GSDMD), and NETs formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G measuring IL-1β in BALF.

claim: Therapeutic hypothermia at 32°C reduced gasdermin D (GSDMD) in LPS-HVV mice.
source: In LPS-HVV mice, TH (32°C body temperature) prevented hypoxemia development, reducing albumin leakage, IL-1β, gasdermin D (GSDMD), and NETs formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6L measuring soluble GSDMD in BALF.

claim: Therapeutic hypothermia at 32°C reduced NETs formation in LPS-HVV mice.
source: In LPS-HVV mice, TH (32°C body temperature) prevented hypoxemia development, reducing albumin leakage, IL-1β, gasdermin D (GSDMD), and NETs formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6N measuring MPO-DNA complexes.

claim: LPS-primed macrophages stimulated at 32°C with ATP or nigericin release less IL-1β compared to 37°C.
source: We also observed that LPS-primed macrophages, when stimulated at 32°C with ATP or nigericin, release less IL-1β associated with reduced GSDMD cleavage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B measuring IL-1β in supernatants.

claim: LPS-primed macrophages stimulated at 32°C with ATP or nigericin have reduced GSDMD cleavage compared to 37°C.
source: We also observed that LPS-primed macrophages, when stimulated at 32°C with ATP or nigericin, release less IL-1β associated with reduced GSDMD cleavage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F-H showing GSDMD immunofluorescence and western blots.

claim: Hypothermia is an important modulating factor in the NLRP3 inflammasome activation.
source: Thus, hypothermia is an important modulating factor in the NLRP3 inflammasome activation, IL-1β release, and NETs formation, preventing LPS-HVV-induced acute respiratory failure.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced IL-1β and GSDMD at 32°C.

claim: Hypothermia modulates IL-1β release.
source: Thus, hypothermia is an important modulating factor in the NLRP3 inflammasome activation, IL-1β release, and NETs formation, preventing LPS-HVV-induced acute respiratory failure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Hypothermia modulates NETs formation.
source: Thus, hypothermia is an important modulating factor in the NLRP3 inflammasome activation, IL-1β release, and NETs formation, preventing LPS-HVV-induced acute respiratory failure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6N and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Hypothermia prevents LPS-HVV-induced acute respiratory failure.
source: Thus, hypothermia is an important modulating factor in the NLRP3 inflammasome activation, IL-1β release, and NETs formation, preventing LPS-HVV-induced acute respiratory failure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing preserved PaO2 in hypothermia-treated mice (Figure 6C).

claim: ARDS is a serious pulmonary disorder defined by the onset of non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema and hypoxemia.
source: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a serious pulmonary disorder defined by the onset of non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema and hypoxemia (Force et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Force et al., 2012.

claim: ARDS is still a major cause of respiratory failure in critically ill patients.
source: While it has been more than 50 years since ARDS was first described in the literature, ARDS is still a major cause of respiratory failure in critically ill patients (Matthay et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Matthay et al., 2019.

claim: Positive-pressure mechanical ventilation has become an essential supportive strategy for the management of ARDS.
source: Positive-pressure mechanical ventilation (MV) has become an essential supportive strategy for the management of ARDS (Del Sorbo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Del Sorbo et al., 2017.

claim: MV itself can cause and aggravate lung injury, a condition termed ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI).
source: However, with the onset of MV as a treatment, it was eventually understood that MV itself can cause and aggravate lung injury, a condition termed ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI) (Rittayamai and Brochard, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rittayamai and Brochard, 2015.

claim: The protective ventilation strategy using low tidal volume has been proven to decrease mortality of ARDS.
source: Although the protective ventilation strategy using low tidal volume has been proven to decrease mortality of ARDS (Pham and Rubenfeld, 2017), the mortality rate of ARDS remains as high as 40% (Bellani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pham and Rubenfeld, 2017.

claim: The mortality rate of ARDS remains as high as 40%.
source: Although the protective ventilation strategy using low tidal volume has been proven to decrease mortality of ARDS (Pham and Rubenfeld, 2017), the mortality rate of ARDS remains as high as 40% (Bellani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bellani et al., 2016.

claim: Non-injurious MV was reported to be able to still activate proinflammatory signals in the lung.
source: Non-injurious MV was reported to be able to still activate proinflammatory signals in the lung (Gharib et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gharib et al., 2009.

claim: Neutrophils are key players in the development of ARDS and VILI.
source: Neutrophils are key players in the development of ARDS and VILI, as their infiltration is a hallmark of lung injury progression (Grommes and Soehnlein, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grommes and Soehnlein, 2011.

claim: Neutrophil infiltration is a hallmark of lung injury progression.
source: Neutrophils are key players in the development of ARDS and VILI, as their infiltration is a hallmark of lung injury progression (Grommes and Soehnlein, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grommes and Soehnlein, 2011.

claim: NETs are a neutrophil-derived meshwork of chromatin fibers decorated with granule peptides and enzymes.
source: NETs are a neutrophil-derived meshwork of chromatin fibers decorated with granule peptides and enzymes and represent a critical host defense strategy against invading microorganisms (Castanheira and Kubes, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Castanheira and Kubes, 2019.

claim: NETs represent a critical host defense strategy against invading microorganisms.
source: NETs are a neutrophil-derived meshwork of chromatin fibers decorated with granule peptides and enzymes and represent a critical host defense strategy against invading microorganisms (Castanheira and Kubes, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Castanheira and Kubes, 2019.

claim: NETs play a role in the pathogenesis of tissue injuries, including ARDS and VILI, either with or without infection.
source: Intriguingly, recent studies found that NETs play a role in the pathogenesis of tissue injuries, including ARDS and VILI, either with or without infection (Porto and Stein, 2016), and NETs have emerged as an important player in COVID-19 pathogenesis (Silva et al., 2022; Veras et al., 2020; Castanheira and Kubes, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Porto and Stein, 2016.

claim: NETs have emerged as an important player in COVID-19 pathogenesis.
source: Intriguingly, recent studies found that NETs play a role in the pathogenesis of tissue injuries, including ARDS and VILI, either with or without infection (Porto and Stein, 2016), and NETs have emerged as an important player in COVID-19 pathogenesis (Silva et al., 2022; Veras et al., 2020; Castanheira and Kubes, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Silva et al., 2022; Veras et al., 2020; Castanheira and Kubes, 2023.

claim: IL-1β levels in BALF were increased in patients with ventilator-associated pneumonia.
source: IL-1β levels in BALF were increased in patients with ventilator-associated pneumonia (Conway Morris et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Conway Morris et al., 2010.

claim: Plasma levels of IL-1β have been associated with worse outcomes in ARDS patients.
source: Furthermore, plasma levels of IL-1β have been associated with worse outcomes in ARDS patients (Meduri et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meduri et al., 1995.

claim: NLRP3 inflammasome activation and interleukin (IL)-1β release by alveolar macrophages was identified as a mechanism for severe acute lung injury development in a two-hit model of ARDS using lipopolysaccharide (LPS) instillation and MV.
source: NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome activation and interleukin (IL)-1β release by alveolar macrophages (AMs) was identified as a mechanism for severe acute lung injury (ALI) development in a two-hit model of ARDS using lipopolysaccharide (LPS) instillation and MV (Jones et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jones et al., 2014.

claim: IL-1β is the most biologically active cytokine in the acute phase of ARDS.
source: IL-1β is the most biologically active cytokine in the acute phase of ARDS.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Mature IL-1β signals via alveolar epithelial cells, resulting in increased lung permeability and pulmonary edema.
source: It is generally considered that mature IL-1β signals via alveolar epithelial cells, resulting in increased lung permeability and pulmonary edema (Ganter et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ganter et al., 2008.

claim: IL-1β and NETs share gasdermin D (GSDMD) as a facilitator of their release.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated that IL-1β and NETs share gasdermin D (GSDMD) as a facilitator of their release (He et al., 2015; Sollberger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to He et al., 2015; Sollberger et al., 2018.

claim: IL-1β promotes NETs formation in different experimental settings.
source: Furthermore, IL-1β promotes NETs formation in different experimental settings, which has attracted attention as an uncovered function of IL-1β (Mitroulis et al., 2011; Apostolidou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mitroulis et al., 2011; Apostolidou et al., 2016.

claim: TH has long been known to be protective against severe lung injuries clinically and experimentally.
source: TH has long been known to be protective against severe lung injuries clinically and experimentally (Villar and Slutsky, 1993; Hayek et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Villar and Slutsky, 1993; Hayek et al., 2017.

claim: In a porcine two-hit model induced by MV and oleic acid, TH reduced the ARDS-associated lung injury and inflammation.
source: In a porcine two-hit model induced by MV and oleic acid, TH reduced the ARDS-associated lung injury and inflammation (Angus et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Angus et al., 2022.

claim: TH has strong anti-inflammatory effects.
source: TH has strong anti-inflammatory effects, and previous studies have reported inhibition of IL-1β production under hypothermia (Diao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Diao et al., 2020.

claim: Previous studies have reported inhibition of IL-1β production under hypothermia.
source: TH has strong anti-inflammatory effects, and previous studies have reported inhibition of IL-1β production under hypothermia (Diao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Diao et al., 2020.

claim: The combination of LPS and HVV (LPS-HVV) caused a prominent reduction in the partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) in the arterial blood of mice when compared to the other controls receiving normal saline (NS) and/or LVV instillation.
source: The combination of LPS and HVV (LPS-HVV) caused a prominent reduction in the partial pressure of oxygen (Figure 1B) in the arterial blood (PaO2) of mice when compared to the other controls receiving normal saline (NS) and/or LVV instillation, indicative of lung dysfunction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The requirement of both LPS and HVV for hypoxemia development was confirmed by the strong interaction (p<0.001) between these two factors.
source: The requirement of both LPS and HVV for hypoxemia development was confirmed by the strong interaction (p<0.001) between these two factors found by the statistical analysis, and it occurred without significant change in carbon dioxide partial pressure (PaCO2), pH, and base excess in the arterial blood (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Hypoxemia occurred without significant change in carbon dioxide partial pressure (PaCO2), pH, and base excess in the arterial blood.
source: The requirement of both LPS and HVV for hypoxemia development was confirmed by the strong interaction (p<0.001) between these two factors found by the statistical analysis, and it occurred without significant change in carbon dioxide partial pressure (PaCO2), pH, and base excess in the arterial blood (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Hypoxemia was accompanied by increased neutrophil migration compared with NS+HVV.
source: Hypoxemia was accompanied by increased neutrophil migration (Figure 1C) compared with NS+HVV without significant change in the number of macrophages (Figure 1D) as determined by flow cytometry (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and in the total cell number (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) in BALF.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Only LPS, but not HVV, was required for the increase of IL-6, TNFα, and CXCL1.
source: Only LPS, but not HVV, was required for the increase of IL-6, TNFα, and CXCL1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–H.

claim: Only HVV was sufficient to increase the IL-18 release.
source: On the other hand, only HVV was sufficient to increase the IL-18 release (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: LPS+HVV increased albumin levels in the BALF, indicating increased vascular permeability.
source: Although these increased inflammatory mediators do not indicate interactions between LPS and HVV in the proposed model, LPS+HVV increased albumin levels in the BALF (Figure 1E), indicating increased vascular permeability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: LPS-HVV injury was associated with increased IL-1β in the BALF.
source: This injury was associated with increased IL-1β (Figure 1F), IL-1α (Figure 1G), CXCL2 (Figure 1H), plasminogen (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J), and fibrinogen (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K) in the BALF.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: LPS-HVV significantly increased MPO and NE, two neutrophil granule enzymes which are also known to contribute to the formation of NETs.
source: We measured the concentration of myeloperoxidase (MPO) (Figure 1I) and neutrophil elastase (NE) (Figure 1J), two neutrophil granule enzymes which are also known to contribute to the formation of NETs (Papayannopoulos et al., 2010; Metzler et al., 2014), as well as the presence of histone-DNA (Figure 1K) and MPO-DNA (Figure 1L) complexes, validated methods for estimating general cell death and NETs (Ishii et al., 2000; Yoo et al., 2014), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and 1J, and citations to Papayannopoulos et al., 2010; Metzler et al., 2014.

claim: LPS-HVV significantly increased histone-DNA and MPO-DNA complexes.
source: We found that LPS-HVV significantly increased all these NETs-associated parameters, indicating the involvement of NETs in the alveolar space with the local severe ALI, resulting in hypoxemia observed in this model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K and 1L.

claim: Neutrophil depletion prevented hypoxemia during LPS-HVV.
source: Neutrophil depletion prevented hypoxemia during LPS-HVV, while mice receiving isotype control antibody developed hypoxemia as before (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The absence of neutrophils significantly reduced the concentration of albumin and IL-6 in BALF.
source: Moreover, in mice depleted of neutrophils, the number of macrophages was quite similar (Figure 2E). The absence of neutrophils significantly reduced the concentration of albumin and IL-6 in BALF (Figure 2F and H), but did not affect the amount of IL-1β and TNFα (Figure 2G and I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and 2H.

claim: The absence of neutrophils did not affect the amount of IL-1β and TNFα in BALF.
source: The absence of neutrophils significantly reduced the concentration of albumin and IL-6 in BALF (Figure 2F and H), but did not affect the amount of IL-1β and TNFα (Figure 2G and I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and 2I.

claim: Neutrophil depletion resulted in lower MPO and NE concentrations in BALF.
source: As expected, neutrophil depletion also resulted in lower MPO and NE concentrations (Figure 2K and L), as well as reduced detection of cell death and NETs (Figure 2M and N) in the BALF.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K and 2L.

claim: Neutrophil depletion resulted in reduced detection of cell death and NETs in the BALF.
source: As expected, neutrophil depletion also resulted in lower MPO and NE concentrations (Figure 2K and L), as well as reduced detection of cell death and NETs (Figure 2M and N) in the BALF.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2M and 2N.

claim: Neutrophil-specific PAD4 deletion significantly inhibited the hypoxemia development compared with control mice.
source: Neutrophil-specific PAD4 deletion significantly inhibited the hypoxemia development compared with control mice (Figure 3B) but without affecting the numbers of neutrophils (Figure 3C) and macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) in the alveoli.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PAD4 deficiency in neutrophils resulted in reduced levels of BALF albumin.
source: It also resulted in reduced levels of BALF albumin but did not change the IL-1β amount in the BALF (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PAD4 deficiency in neutrophils did not change the IL-1β amount in the BALF.
source: It also resulted in reduced levels of BALF albumin but did not change the IL-1β amount in the BALF (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: PAD4 deficiency in neutrophils reduced NETs formation as measured by MPO-DNA complexes.
source: PAD4 deficiency in neutrophils did not alter the levels of MPO and NE in BALF (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D) but did reduce cell death as measured by histone DNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and NETs formation as measured by MPO-DNA complexes (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: DNase I treatment significantly prevented hypoxemia.
source: This intervention also significantly prevented hypoxemia (Figure 3H) with no impact on neutrophil migration (Figure 3I) and number of macrophage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: DNase I treatment reduced the albumin leakage.
source: It also reduced the albumin leakage (Figure 3J) without altering IL-1β levels (Figure 3K) in the alveoli.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: DNase I treatment did not alter IL-1β levels in the alveoli.
source: It also reduced the albumin leakage (Figure 3J) without altering IL-1β levels (Figure 3K) in the alveoli.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: DNase I treatment resulted in efficiently reduced NETs formation as measured by MPO-DNA complexes.
source: We observed that DNase I treatment resulted in similar levels of MPO and NE (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I) and resulted in efficiently reduced cell death as measured by histone DNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J) and NETs formation as measured by MPO-DNA complexes (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Loss of IL-1R1 prevented the development of edema resulting from increased vascular permeability, as measured by albumin in BALF.
source: Although IL1R1 deficiency did not affect the number of neutrophils and macrophages in BALF (Figure 4C and D), it prevented the development of edema resulting from increased vascular permeability, as measured by albumin in BALF (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Loss of IL-1R1 led to a reduction in BALF MPO and NE levels.
source: Even though the lack of IL-1R1 did not affect neutrophil migration, its loss led to a reduction in BALF MPO and NE levels (Figure 4J and K), as well as cell death (histone DNA) and the NETs formation as measured by MPO-DNA complexes in the BALF (Figure 4L and M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J and 4K.

claim: Loss of IL-1R1 led to a reduction in cell death and NETs formation in the BALF.
source: Even though the lack of IL-1R1 did not affect neutrophil migration, its loss led to a reduction in BALF MPO and NE levels (Figure 4J and K), as well as cell death (histone DNA) and the NETs formation as measured by MPO-DNA complexes in the BALF (Figure 4L and M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4L and 4M.

claim: IL-1β, but not LPS, enhanced ION-induced NETs formation of both BMN and AN.
source: We found that IL-1β, but not LPS, enhanced ION-induced NETs formation of both BMN (Figure 5C and D) and AN (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C, D, F, and G.

claim: Hypothermia resulted in reduced levels of BALF MPO and NE.
source: While similar neutrophil and macrophage counts were observed between the two groups (Figure 6D and E), hypothermia resulted in reduced levels of BALF albumin, IL-1β, IL-6, TNFα, MPO, and NE (Figure 6F–K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6J and 6K.

claim: Soluble GSDMD concentration in the BALF was significantly diminished in mice ventilated under hypothermia.
source: GSDMD-mediated pore formation impacts not only IL-1β release by macrophages but was also described to play a role in NETs formation (Sollberger et al., 2018). We therefore evaluated the soluble GSDMD concentration in the BALF by ELISA (Figure 6L) and found it significantly diminished in mice ventilated under hypothermia.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6L and citation to Sollberger et al., 2018.

claim: Hypothermia significantly inhibited the presence of cell death and NETs formation in the BALF in mice subjected to LPS-HVV.
source: We observed that hypothermia also significantly inhibited the presence of cell death and NETs formation in the BALF in mice subjected to LPS-HVV (Figure 6M and N).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6M and 6N.

claim: Neither alkalosis nor acidosis was observed during hypothermia treatment.
source: Finally, neither alkalosis (blood pH>7.45) nor acidosis (blood pH<7.35) was observed during hypothermia treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The mechanism by which hypothermia inhibits IL-1β release seems to be independent of caspase-1 activation.
source: The mechanism by which hypothermia inhibits IL-1β release seems to be independent of caspase-1 activation, as there was no difference in caspase-1 activity assay by FLICA between 37°C or 32°C treated macrophages (Figure 7C and D), but we found that hypothermia resulted in reduced caspase-1 release in the supernatant (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing no difference in caspase-1 activity but reduced caspase-1 release.

claim: At 32°C BMDMs express less GSDMD with reduced GSDMD cleavage.
source: Thus, we investigated the effect of 37°C or 32°C temperature on GSDMD expression and cleavage in BMDMs by immunofluorescence and observed that at 32°C BMDMs express less GSDMD with reduced GSDMD cleavage (Figure 7F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F–H.

claim: 32°C treatment inhibited GSDMD secretion.
source: Furthermore, 32°C treatment inhibited GSDMD secretion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E and H.

claim: While hypothermia inhibited the IL-1β release in the supernatant, there was a concomitant accumulation of unreleased mature IL-1β in the macrophages incubated at 32°C.
source: These data corroborated our observation that while hypothermia inhibited the IL-1β release in the supernatant, there was a concomitant accumulation of unreleased mature IL-1β in the macrophages incubated at 32°C (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Hypothermic condition (32°C temperature) significantly inhibited IL-1β release even in macrophages with impaired autophagy.
source: To identify whether hypothermia regulates IL-1β release by inducing autophagy, we isolated BMDMs from Atg16l1fl/fl or Atg16l1fl/fl Lyz2Cre+ mice and repeated the previous experiment. Hypothermic condition (32°C temperature) again significantly inhibited IL-1β release even in macrophages with impaired autophagy, suggesting that the hypothermia effect is independent of autophagy (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and predominantly through diminished activation of GSDMD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The hypothermia effect is independent of autophagy and predominantly through diminished activation of GSDMD.
source: Hypothermic condition (32°C temperature) again significantly inhibited IL-1β release even in macrophages with impaired autophagy, suggesting that the hypothermia effect is independent of autophagy (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and predominantly through diminished activation of GSDMD.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing IL-1β inhibition in autophagy-deficient cells and reduced GSDMD.

claim: Significantly reduced NETs formation was observed in both BMN and AN stimulated at 32°C when compared to experiments conducted at 37°C.
source: We observed significantly reduced NETs formation in both BMN and AN stimulated at 32°C when compared to experiments conducted at 37°C (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: IL-1β plays a significant role as a driver of the vicious cycle involved in ventilation-induced ALI and ARDS.
source: Our data support and expand the premise that IL-1β plays a significant role as a driver of the vicious cycle involved in ventilation-induced ALI and ARDS.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing IL-1β's role in NETs formation and lung injury.

claim: PADs are required for NETs formation.
source: In the first, we used neutrophil-specific PAD4-deficient (Padi4Δ/Δ S100a8cre) mice and controls (Padi4fl/fl) (Figure 3A). PADs are required for NETs formation (Rohrbach et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rohrbach et al., 2012.

claim: Cleavage of GSDMD is a late limiting step for inflammasome-mediated IL-1β release.
source: Cleavage of GSDMD is a late limiting step for inflammasome-mediated IL-1β release because its N-terminal fragment forms pores on macrophages' plasma membrane where the intracellular cytokine crosses into the extracellular compartment (He et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al., 2015.

claim: The N-terminal fragment of GSDMD forms pores on macrophages' plasma membrane where the intracellular cytokine crosses into the extracellular compartment.
source: Cleavage of GSDMD is a late limiting step for inflammasome-mediated IL-1β release because its N-terminal fragment forms pores on macrophages' plasma membrane where the intracellular cytokine crosses into the extracellular compartment (He et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al., 2015.

claim: Hypothermia attenuated the expression of caspase-1 in traumatic brain injury in rats, with reduced mature IL-1β and caspase-1 in the cerebral cortex.
source: Another study reported that hypothermia attenuated the expression of caspase-1 in traumatic brain injury in rats, with reduced mature IL-1β and caspase-1 in the cerebral cortex (Tomura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tomura et al., 2012.

claim: The cleaved N-terminus GSDMD can form oligomeric pores in the plasma membrane and play a key role in IL-1β secretion.
source: It has been broadly proposed that the cleaved N-terminus GSDMD can form oligomeric pores in the plasma membrane and play a key role in IL-1β secretion (Zou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zou et al., 2021.

claim: LPS-dependent palmitoylation was proposed as a requirement for N-terminus GSDMD pore formation in macrophages.
source: While LPS-dependent palmitoylation was proposed as a requirement for N-terminus GSDMD pore formation in macrophages (Balasubramanian et al., 2024), the N-terminus GSDMD plasma membrane translocation and pore formation mechanisms are still poorly understood.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Balasubramanian et al., 2024.

claim: GSDMD binds to mitochondria outer membrane and nuclei besides plasma membrane.
source: Indeed, GSDMD binds to mitochondria outer membrane (Yu et al., 2022; Miao et al., 2023) and nuclei (He et al., 2023) besides plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yu et al., 2022; Miao et al., 2023; He et al., 2023.

claim: Soluble GSDMD is detected in culture supernatant or body fluids.
source: Furthermore, several studies have shown that soluble GSDMD is detected in culture supernatant or body fluids (Karmakar et al., 2020; Nagai et al., 2021; Silva et al., 2022), but our study may be the first reporting GSDMD detection in the BALF in LPS plus MV-induced severe ALI.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Karmakar et al., 2020; Nagai et al., 2021; Silva et al., 2022.

claim: This study may be the first reporting GSDMD detection in the BALF in LPS plus MV-induced severe ALI.
source: Furthermore, several studies have shown that soluble GSDMD is detected in culture supernatant or body fluids (Karmakar et al., 2020; Nagai et al., 2021; Silva et al., 2022), but our study may be the first reporting GSDMD detection in the BALF in LPS plus MV-induced severe ALI.
evidence: This is speculative based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: GSDMD can participate in the host defense by binding to pathogen membranes, potentially forming cytotoxic pores.
source: Supporting this, GSDMD can participate in the host defense by binding to pathogen membranes, potentially forming cytotoxic pores (Lieberman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lieberman et al., 2019.

claim: Mortality in patients with ARDS does not differ between sexes.
source: However, despite this limitation, we believe these results to be generally applicable as human studies have found that mortality in patients with ARDS does not differ between sexes (Heffernan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heffernan et al., 2011.

claim: LPS induces a febrile response in humans.
source: Moreover, LPS induces a febrile response in humans (Ganeshan and Chawla, 2017) and can cause either hyperthermia or hypothermia in mice, depending on the dose and ambient temperature (Rudaya et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ganeshan and Chawla, 2017.

claim: LPS can cause either hyperthermia or hypothermia in mice, depending on the dose and ambient temperature.
source: Moreover, LPS induces a febrile response in humans (Ganeshan and Chawla, 2017) and can cause either hyperthermia or hypothermia in mice, depending on the dose and ambient temperature (Rudaya et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rudaya et al., 2005.

claim: Mice and humans differ in their sensitivity to LPS.
source: Mice and humans also differ in their sensitivity to LPS (Ganeshan and Chawla, 2017), highlighting limitations when translating these findings to human sepsis or infection responses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ganeshan and Chawla, 2017.

claim: The inflammasome pathway and its downstream mediators, such as IL-1β and NETosis, may be effective therapeutic targets and could be downmodulated by hypothermia during management of ARDS.
source: These observations suggest that the inflammasome pathway and its downstream mediators, such as IL-1β and NETosis, may be effective therapeutic targets and could be downmodulated by hypothermia during management of ARDS.
evidence: This is speculative based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.
